faqs.question: How much is the entrance ticket to Karnak Temple?
faqs.answer: Foreign adults pay approximately 600 EGP, with a discounted rate of around 300 EGP for foreign students with valid ID. Egyptian nationals pay significantly less. Prices are subject to periodic revision by the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities.

faqs.question: What are Karnak Temple's opening hours?
faqs.answer: Karnak is typically open from around 6:00 am to 5:30 pm in winter (October–April) and until about 6:00 pm in summer (May–September), though exact hours can vary slightly.

faqs.question: Why is Karnak Temple so large compared to other Egyptian temples?
faqs.answer: Karnak was continuously expanded by successive pharaohs over roughly 2,000 years, from the Middle Kingdom through the Ptolemaic period, rather than being built by a single ruler in one campaign, making it the largest religious complex in the ancient world.

faqs.question: What is the Great Hypostyle Hall?
faqs.answer: It is Karnak's most famous feature: a vast hall containing 134 massive sandstone columns arranged in 16 rows, largely built under Seti I and completed by Ramesses II, with the tallest central columns reaching about 21 meters high.

faqs.question: Which god was Karnak dedicated to?
faqs.answer: Karnak was primarily dedicated to Amun-Ra, king of the gods in the Theban region, along with his consort Mut and their son Khonsu, together known as the Theban triad.

faqs.question: Is there a Sound and Light Show at Karnak?
faqs.answer: Yes, Karnak hosts an evening Sound and Light Show that narrates the temple's history while illuminating its columns, obelisks, and halls. Shows run at staggered times with rotating language narration, and tickets are purchased separately from daytime entry.

faqs.question: How long does it take to visit Karnak Temple?
faqs.answer: Most visitors spend 1.5 to 3 hours exploring the main precinct and Great Hypostyle Hall; history enthusiasts wanting to see the outer precincts as well may want longer.

faqs.question: Is Karnak connected to Luxor Temple?
faqs.answer: Yes, the two temples were historically linked by a roughly 2.7 km processional avenue lined with sphinxes, known as the Avenue of Sphinxes, sections of which have been excavated and restored for visitors.

faqs.question: What is the best time of day to visit Karnak?
faqs.answer: Early morning right at opening offers cooler temperatures and fewer tour groups; late afternoon after large groups depart is another good window. Midday hours combine peak heat and crowds and are best avoided.

faqs.question: Can I combine a visit to Karnak with the Valley of the Kings?
faqs.answer: Yes, many full-day Luxor tours combine Karnak and Luxor Temple on the East Bank with the Valley of the Kings and Hatshepsut's Temple on the West Bank, though this typically requires a full day given travel between banks.

faqs.question: What is the sacred lake at Karnak?
faqs.answer: It is a large rectangular lake within the temple precinct that ancient priests used for ritual purification before religious ceremonies; it remains a prominent feature of the site today.

faqs.question: Are there obelisks still standing at Karnak?
faqs.answer: Yes, several obelisks remain, including ones erected by Hatshepsut and Thutmose I, some of the tallest surviving ancient Egyptian obelisks still in their original location.

faqs.question: How far is Karnak from Cairo?
faqs.answer: Karnak Temple is about 645 km south of Cairo. Most visitors reach Luxor by a roughly one-hour domestic flight or an overnight sleeper train from Cairo.

faqs.question: Is photography allowed inside Karnak Temple?
faqs.answer: Non-flash photography with standard cameras and phones is generally permitted throughout the complex, including inside the Great Hypostyle Hall. Tripods and professional video equipment typically require a separate paid permit.

faqs.question: Is Karnak suitable for visitors with mobility issues?
faqs.answer: Much of the site has flat paved or packed-earth paths, but some inner areas feature uneven ancient stone flooring, which can make full wheelchair access to every part of the temple difficult.
